supplementary_news.content: Skip to main content Global editionFriday, October 2, 2026 Streamline Search⌘KWriteSign inJoin Streamline StreamlineGlobal edition LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSportDirectoryHouse HuntingPeopleHistoryMore LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSport Back to News/Health Health One in eight global cancer cases linked to infections, IARC study finds An estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 were caused by preventable infections, with H. pylori and HPV driving the new global burden. Streamline Feed OfficialVerified Sep 29, 2026Updated Sep 29, 20264 min read Report article Follow on Google News Try askingWhy does this matter? Advertisement from Streamline Feed. The first 10 seconds cannot be skipped. Ad playing Ad playing. Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% One in eight new cancer cases diagnosed worldwide in 2024 was caused by infections, according to a comprehensive new analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). The study, published in The Lancet Oncology, estimates that approximately 2.3 million cancers are attributable to infectious agents, highlighting a massive and largely preventable burden on global health systems. The findings underscore that while tobacco and metabolic risks dominate cancer prevention campaigns in high-income nations, infections remain a primary driver of malignancies in vast regions of the developing world. The primary infectious drivers The greatest cancer burden was linked to Helicobacter pylori, a common stomach bacter responsible for an estimated 760,000 cancer cases in 2024. H. pylori is a known cause of gastric cancer, and its prevalence remains high in regions with limited access to early screening and antibiotic eradication therapies. Closely following the bacterium are human papillomavirus (HPV) and the hepatitis B and C viruses. HPV remains the primary cause of cervical cancer, which continues to claim hundreds of thousands of lives annually, predominantly in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Hepatitis B and C, meanwhile, drive a significant proportion of liver cancer cases globally. Researchers utilized data from the IARC Global Cancer Observatory's GLOBOCAN 2024 database to calculate population-attributable fractions across 12 infectious agents classified as Group 1 carcinogens. The Epstein-Barr virus and Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus also contributed to the global tally, though their absolute numbers were smaller than the primary bacterial and viral drivers. Geographic disparities and prevention gaps The analysis reveals stark geographic inequities in how infections translate into cancer diagnoses. In high-income countries, infection-related cancers represent a small fraction of the total disease burden, largely mitigated by widespread childhood vaccination programs, blood supply screening, and access to antiviral medications. In contrast, lower-income nations bear a disproportionate share of the global infection-attributable cancer burden. The absence of routine HPV vaccination for adolescent girls, limited hepatitis B birth-dose coverage, and a lack of curative direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C mean that millions of preventable cancers are locked in decades before they manifest. Public health experts note that the latency period between chronic infection and cancer development means the 2024 incidence figures reflect transmission and healthcare gaps that persisted in the 1990s and early 2000s. Consequently, current vaccination efforts will not fully register in global cancer statistics until the 2040s or 2050s. Shifting the prevention paradigm The IARC findings present a clear utility for global health policy: the tools to prevent millions of cancer cases already exist. Unlike lifestyle interventions, which require complex behavioral shifts, infection-related cancers can be addressed through established medical infrastructure. The World Health Organization has already set global targets to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem through the 90-70-90 strategy, which relies heavily on HPV vaccination and screening. Similarly, hepatitis C can now be cured with short courses of oral medications, and hepatitis B can be suppressed to drastically reduce liver cancer risk. However, the logistical challenge remains formidable. Reaching rural populations with multi-dose vaccine schedules, securing cold-chain storage in tropical climates, and overcoming vaccine hesitancy require sustained domestic health financing and international aid. The study concludes that integrating cancer prevention into existing infectious disease programs could yield some of the highest returns on investment in modern oncology. Biological mechanisms of carcinogenesis The link between chronic infection and cancer is rooted in prolonged inflammation and direct cellular interference. H. pylori, for instance, induces chronic gastritis that can progress to atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia, creating an environment where DNA damage accumulates and malignant cells proliferate. Viral carcinogens operate through different pathways. High-risk strains of HPV produce oncoproteins that disable host tumor suppressor genes, allowing infected cervical cells to divide uncontrollably. Hepatitis viruses promote liver cancer through cycles of necrosis and regeneration, accelerating the mutation rate of hepatocytes. Understanding these mechanisms has allowed researchers to identify precise intervention points. For example, the development of highly sensitive blood tests for circulating tumor DNA is now being explored as a way to detect infection-associated cancers earlier in high-risk populations, potentially bridging the gap between infection management and oncology. Methodology and study limitations The Lancet Oncology analysis relied on national cancer registry data and mortality estimates, which vary significantly in quality across different jurisdictions. In many low- and middle-income countries, cancer registries cover only small urban populations, requiring IARC statisticians to model national incidence based on regional sampling. Furthermore, the study focuses exclusively on Group 1 carcinogens—agents for which there is sufficient evidence of carcinogenicity in humans. Emerging research suggests that the human microbiome as a whole, including non-classified bacterial flora, may influence cancer susceptibility and treatment efficacy, a frontier that current epidemiological models do not yet capture. Despite these limitations, the 2024 GLOBOCAN estimates provide the most authoritative baseline to date. By isolating the infectious fraction of the global cancer burden, the IARC study offers policymakers a quantifiable target: scaling up existing vaccines and antimicrobial therapies could fundamentally alter the trajectory of global oncology over the next half-century. Updated: 5:28 PM EDT Oct 2, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jessica Brown Anchor/Reporter Ed Harding Anchor WEYMOUTH, Mass. — Many people think of infections as illnesses that come and go. But some viruses and bacteria can increase the risk of developing certain cancers years — or even decades — later. Dr. Todd Ellerin of South Shore Health explained which infections are linked to cancer and how many of them can be prevented or treated before they cause long-term harm. Advertisement His message comes as new research published in The Lancet Oncology estimates that infections were responsible for 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024, accounting for about 12% of all cancer diagnoses. The study found the largest number of infection-related cancers were linked to Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), followed closely by human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV). Which infections are linked to cancer? Dr. Ellerin said several well-known infections have been tied to specific cancers. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is linked to most cases of cervical cancer. Hepatitis B and hepatitis C viruses are associated with liver cancer, while a bacterial stomach infection known as Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is linked to gastric cancer. "People are often surprised to learn that infections can lead to cancer years or even decades later," Dr. Ellerin said. The Lancet Oncology study estimated that H. pylori accounted for roughly 760,000 new cancer cases worldwide in 2024, followed by 750,000 linked to HPV, 360,000 to hepatitis B, 260,000 to Epstein-Barr virus and 160,000 to hepatitis C. Researchers said eastern Asia had the highest overall burden of infection-related cancers, while rates were also above the global average in sub-Saharan Africa, central and eastern Europe and southeastern Asia. Prevention can make a difference The researchers behind the Lancet Oncology study said scientifically proven—but often underused—prevention strategies include HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, testing and treatment for HIV, H. pylori, hepatitis B and hepatitis C, safer injection practices, access to condoms and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and screening for precancerous cervical and anal lesions caused by HPV. Is it ever too late? Many people think of these vaccines as something only children receive, but Dr. Ellerin said adults may also be eligible. He explained that the hepatitis B vaccine can be given to adults of any age. The HPV vaccine is recommended for people ages 9 through 26, and some adults at higher risk may be eligible through age 45. "The bottom line is it's never too late to talk to your provider to see if you are eligible," Dr. Ellerin said. "One of the infections prevented today could be cancer prevented a decade from now." If you have questions about your vaccination history or whether you may benefit from vaccination, screening or treatment, talk with your healthcare provider. A new study published in MicrobiologyOpen has used high-throughput 16S rRNA gene sequencing to map the vaginal and cervical microbiota of women with cervical cancer and healthy controls in southern China, revealing a dramatic microbial reconfiguration that accompanies malignancy. The findings add weight to a growing body of evidence that the trillions of microbes inhabiting the reproductive tract are not passive bystanders but active participants in the journey from human papillomavirus (HPV) infection to invasive carcinoma. Cervical cancer remains one of the most significant threats to women’s health worldwide, ranking as the fourth most common malignancy among women globally. More than 600,000 new cases are diagnosed each year, and nearly 90 percent of them occur in resource-limited countries. In China, the disease is increasingly affecting younger women, intensifying the urgency of understanding why some HPV infections resolve quietly while others progress to precancerous lesions and cancer. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV is firmly established as the primary cause, yet only a small fraction of infected women ever develop invasive disease, a discrepancy that has long pointed to additional cofactors. Among those cofactors, the microbial communities of the vagina and cervix have emerged as compelling suspects. In healthy women, the genus Lactobacillus typically dominates the reproductive tract, maintaining an acidic environment, competitively excluding pathogens, and modulating local immune responses. Epidemiological studies have consistently identified bacterial vaginosis, a condition marked by depletion of Lactobacillus and overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria, as a risk factor for cervical neoplasia. However, the molecular mechanisms linking microbial dysbiosis to carcinogenesis, and the specific functional gene programs expressed by cancer-associated bacteria, have remained poorly defined. Conventional culture-based methods, limited in sensitivity and coverage, have also hindered comprehensive characterization of these complex ecosystems. Discover more Biotechnology Job Board Biotechnology Research Updates Biotechnology Newsletters Learn Engineering Track Biotech To address these gaps, researchers recruited women visiting gynecology departments at Nanchong Hospital, Beijing Anzhen Hospital, and Capital Medical University between January and June 2024. After applying strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, 32 women aged 45 to 65 were enrolled and stratified by vaginal discharge microscopy and cervical biopsy histopathology into 16 cervical cancer patients and 16 healthy controls. Crucially, all cancer patients tested positive for high-risk HPV while all controls were HPV-negative, providing a clean contrast that allowed the team to attribute microbial shifts specifically to HPV-driven disease. Women with recent antibiotic use, vaginal douching, bacterial vaginosis, sexually transmitted infections, prior cervical lesions, or systemic diseases were excluded, minimizing confounding. The team collected sterile swabs from both the vaginal wall and the cervical os during gynecological examinations, extracted genomic DNA, and amplified the hypervariable V3-V4 region of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina MiSeq platform with paired-end 300-base reads, and the data were processed using the DADA2 algorithm within the QIIME 2 framework to denoise reads, merge pairs, remove chimeras, and construct amplicon sequence variants. Taxonomic annotation relied on a pre-trained Naive Bayes classifier against the Greengenes reference database. After quality filtering excluded three samples from each group, 13 participants per group formed the final analytical cohort, which was well matched for body mass index, pregnancies, menstrual characteristics, and other clinical variables. Discover more Science Education Resources Cancer Support Resources genetic The compositional results were striking. Healthy controls were uniformly dominated by Lactobacillus, with a median relative abundance of 72.5 percent and minimal variation between individuals. In cervical cancer patients, Lactobacillus abundance collapsed to a median of just 12.5 percent, a highly significant difference. In its place, anaerobic genera flourished: Prevotella rose from a median of 6.8 percent in controls to 28.3 percent in cancer patients, while Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, Enterococcus, and Corynebacterium were also enriched. The cancer group showed higher overall microbial diversity, greater inter-individual variability, and, notably, site-specific heterogeneity between the vaginal wall and cervical os, whereas healthy women maintained stable communities across both anatomical sites. Diversity metrics reinforced this picture of ecological disruption. Species richness indices such as Chao1 and observed species did not differ between groups, indicating that cancer samples did not simply gain or lose bacterial types but instead underwent a wholesale shift in community composition. Pielou’s evenness was significantly lower in cancer patients, while Shannon and Simpson indices and Faith’s phylogenetic diversity were all elevated, reflecting colonization by multiple opportunistic pathogens and a fragmented community structure following the collapse of the Lactobacillus-dominated stable state. Analysis of similarities based on Bray-Curtis distances confirmed a statistically significant, though moderate, separation between the groups, with an R-value of 0.218 and a p-value of 0.001. When the cancer patients were subdivided by HPV genotype into HPV16-positive and HPV-positive/non-16 subgroups, community structure remained comparable between the two, suggesting that high-risk HPV infection as a whole, rather than any particular subtype, exerts the dominant selective pressure on the cervical microenvironment. Discover more Learn AI Tools Genetic Disease Information Find Cancer Care Genetic Testing Services scientific Network analysis and functional prediction pushed the findings beyond taxonomy into mechanism. Co-occurrence networks built with the SparCC algorithm revealed that healthy samples centered on a stable Lactobacillus-driven network, whereas cancer samples displayed a more complex, Prevotella-centered pathogenic network, with Lactobacillus showing widespread negative associations with Prevotella that suggest competitive exclusion between a health-associated commensal and potential pathogens. Functional prediction using PICRUSt2 mapped gene families onto Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathways and revealed that glycolytic flux was significantly elevated in cancer samples, consistent with lactate accumulation and acidification of the tumor microenvironment, while oxidative phosphorylation was diminished, indicating a metabolic shift toward anaerobic fermentation. The aerobactin biosynthesis pathway, which enables bacteria to scavenge iron from the host, was markedly upregulated in the cancer cohort, hinting at a novel link between dysbiosis, iron acquisition, and tumor progression. Meanwhile, reduced representation of antigen-presentation and complement pathways suggested microbial strategies of immune evasion. The study’s authors caution that several limitations temper these conclusions. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, precancerous cases were excluded so microbiota dynamics during lesion progression could not be traced, and 16S rRNA sequencing lacks the species-level resolution needed to fully resolve functional heterogeneity, making metagenomic validation essential. Nevertheless, the results align closely with international findings, including a 2025 meta-analysis confirming elevated Prevotella in cervical cancer patients and cohort studies linking non-Lactobacillus-dominated community state types to persistent high-risk HPV infection and lesion progression. The researchers propose that future work should employ metagenomics to confirm aerobactin genes in enriched taxa, establish HPV-transgenic mouse models colonized with patient-derived Prevotella strains, and test probiotic interventions with Lactobacillus crispatus to restore acidic pH and inhibit pathobionts. If validated in longitudinal cohorts, the microbial signatures identified here, particularly the depletion of Lactobacillus, the enrichment of Prevotella, and the activation of iron-acquisition and inflammatory pathways, could serve as auxiliary biomarkers for early risk prediction and open the door to precision interventions based on microecological remodeling. Daily roundup Spark: Our top stories Just 5 Infections Responsible For More Than 2 Million New Cancer Cases Annually Health29 September 2026 By Jess Cockerill (Kateryna Kon/Science Photo Library RF/Getty Images) Cancer may seem like an inevitable part of life, but there are so many factors that can help reduce your risk. When we think about reducing cancer risk, we usually think of lifestyle factors: smoking, alcohol consumption, exercise. But a new study by a team of cancer epidemiologists, published in The Lancet Oncology, highlights just how much infections actually contribute to your cancer risk. Based on global data, infections were linked to 12 percent of all cancers that were diagnosed in 2024. That's 2.3 million new cancer cases. Five key pathogens were responsible for nearly all of those infection-linked cases. The most common offender was a stomach bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, which was involved in 4 percent of the total cancers diagnosed in 2024 – that's 760,000 cases. H. pylori is a really common bug: statistically speaking, every second person in the world is infected with it. For most people, infection with H. pylori causes no symptoms, but certain strains can cause gastric ulcers and ultimately stomach cancers. The human papillomavirus (HPV) was also linked to 4 percent of the total new cancers diagnosed in 2024, which is 750,000 cases. frameborder="0′′ allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen> Hepatitis B virus (HBV) was linked to 2 percent of new cases, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was linked to 1 percent, and hepatitis C virus (HCV) was linked to less than 1 percent. EBV is a newcomer to this list. Since previous global estimates were published, the evidence that EBV causes cancer has grown substantially. It's pretty freaky to think that these infections, which can already make us very sick in their own right, could also lead to cancer, but these findings also give us an opportunity. They suggest proper treatment and prevention of these infections could make a really big difference to cancer rates across the world. "Our updated estimates highlight the continued importance of infection control in global cancer prevention strategies," lead author Harriet Rumgay and her colleagues note. "Many carcinogenic infectious agents have existing or potential preventive interventions, including vaccines, diagnostics, treatments, and safe injection practices." For many of these pathogens, it's a matter of actually getting those public health interventions to people. "Despite progress in vaccination and screening, infection-related cancers remain a major challenge globally, with persistent inequities especially impacting low-income and middle-income countries," the authors add. Three-quarters of infection-related cancers came from low-income and middle-income countries, predominantly in eastern Asia, African nations south of the Sahara, and southeastern Asia. The bulk of infection-linked cancer diagnoses in 2024 were made in eastern Asia, making up 42 percent of the global total. The infections linked to those diagnoses were mainly H. pylori and HBV. Getting more people vaccinated for HPV (especially men, who have often not been targeted for HPV vaccines) and HBV should make a huge dent in global cancer rates, but for H. pylori, the answer is not so simple. "So far, there has been little progress in developing H. pylori vaccines or highly effective H. pylori therapies that can minimize ineffective antibiotic exposure, which would be highly impactful for controlling gastric cancer globally," the authors write. We also have no vaccine or any other methods to control the spread of EBV (which infects about 95 percent of adults), though several clinical trials for vaccines are underway. "Although investment in the development of new preventive vaccinations for EBV, H. pylori, and Kaposi's sarcoma [another cancer linked to viruses] is key, many prevention strategies are known to be cost-effective," the authors write. "Unfortunately, such strategies are often underused due to societal, financial, and political barriers, often in the settings that need them most. "Considering the overwhelming economic and social costs of cancer, investment in prevention is crucial." The research was published in The Lancet Oncology. This article was fact-checked by Fiona MacDonald and edited by Fiona MacDonald. While we pride ourselves on our process, we are only human. If you spot a mistake, please let us know. Home » English » Lifestyle » Health » Why Getting Vaccinated Against HPV Can Reduce Cancer Risk Why Getting Vaccinated Against HPV Can Reduce Cancer Risk The HPV vaccine can prevent more than 90% of cancers caused by the virus, according to the CDC, find out how it reduces risk. By Kristel Escobar FOTO: Referencial recreada con IA Posted on 09/29/26 at 06:00 HPV: Prevention from an Early Age Protection Against Several Cancers Vaccination for Both Sexes The return to school can also be an opportunity to review a task that often stays out of the backpack: the vaccination of children and adolescents. Among the immunizations with a direct impact on cancer prevention, vaccines against human papillomavirus (HPV) and hepatitis B stand out. Infectious disease specialist and clinical pharmacologist Jorge Chaverri recommended taking advantage of the new 2026-2027 school year to review vaccination schedules and strengthen preventive habits. The recommendation is relevant because some infections acquired during a person’s lifetime can remain silent and, years later, contribute to the development of serious diseases. Why it’s important: HPV can cause cancer in both women and men, and vaccination provides protection before possible exposure to the virus. HPV: A Common Virus Linked to Several Cancers HPV Vaccine and Cancer Prevention: How Vaccination Can Reduce Risk – PHOTO: Shutterstock HPV is a very common infection that can be transmitted through intimate contact and affect people of both sexes, although many infections clear on their own. The problem arises when certain high-risk types persist for years and cause cellular changes that can eventually develop into cancer. According to the CDC, HPV can cause cervical, vaginal, vulvar, penile, anal, and oropharyngeal cancers, including cancers of the back of the throat. U.S. data show the scale of the problem: each year, approximately 49,908 HPV-associated cancers are diagnosed, of which about 39,300 are attributable to the virus. The fact: the CDC estimates that HPV vaccination can prevent more than 90% of cancers caused by this virus. It’s not just women: approximately four out of 10 cancers caused by HPV occur in men. It’s not a treatment: the vaccine prevents new infections but does not eliminate an existing HPV infection. At What Age Should the HPV Vaccine Be Given? Chaverri highlighted the importance of early immunization because the goal is to prepare the body before exposure to the HPV types covered by the vaccine. In the United States, the CDC routinely recommends vaccination at ages 11 or 12, although the series can begin at age 9. Additionally, catch-up vaccination is recommended through age 26 for people who were not adequately vaccinated during childhood or adolescence. For some adults ages 27 to 45, vaccination may be considered after discussing individual risks and potential benefits with a healthcare professional. Important: this differs from statements that present the vaccine as routinely recommended after age 26 or without an age limit; those do not correspond to the CDC’s current recommendations for the United States. The HPV Vaccine Does Not Replace Medical Check-Ups HPV Vaccine and Cancer Prevention: How Vaccination Can Reduce Risk – PHOTO: Shutterstock Being vaccinated also does not mean abandoning preventive check-ups, especially because some abnormalities can develop without producing symptoms for a long time. «What happens is that most cancers really, if we wait for symptoms, we probably arrive late,» warned Chaverri. In the case of cervical cancer, the CDC emphasizes the importance of screening even among vaccinated women because vaccination and early detection serve different purposes. Hepatitis B offers another example of the link between immunization and cancer: its vaccine helps prevent infections that can cause chronic liver disease and liver cancer. The process: reviewing with a pediatrician or healthcare provider which vaccines are recommended based on age, medical history, and doses already received. At home: talking about prevention before adolescence can help normalize health-related decisions. What they can do: keeping vaccination records, reviewing pending doses, and maintaining recommended medical check-ups. For Chaverri, schools and families can also contribute by creating spaces where parents, teachers, and students receive reliable information and can ask questions about vaccination. Prevention, he said, should be complemented by balanced nutrition, exercise, regular check-ups, and open family conversations about health. Thus, a vaccine administered during childhood or adolescence can represent something much greater than fulfilling a preventive requirement: reducing the risk of certain cancers decades later. Warning: This information is for educational purposes and does not replace the evaluation or recommendation of a healthcare professional. supplementary_news.content: Bulgaria World Opinions Business Properties Auto Tech Sport Culture Bulgaria World Opinions Business Properties Auto Tech Sport Culture Cars Properties Jobs Small ads Здраве » Preventable infections cause an estimated 2.3 million additional cases of cancer each year Preventable infections cause an estimated 2.3 million additional cases of cancer each year Approximately one in eight new cancer cases worldwide are due to infections that are often preventable Oct 1, 2026 19:01 105 Sybina Andreeva Author at Fakti.bg Viruses, bacteria and even parasites play a role - approximately one in eight new cancer cases worldwide are due to infections that are often preventable. This can be done through vaccines, although there is still much to be done, especially in less-developed countries, AFP reported, citing the World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer (WHO). As for the global burden of cancer, about 2.3 million additional cases a year are due to infections, representing approximately 12 percent of the total, according to the study published in the journal The Lancet Oncology. "A large proportion of cases of this deadly disease remain linked to infections, but we can often take measures to avoid them, which is not always the case with other types of cancer," Dr. Gary Clifford, its lead co-author, told AFP. This review, which estimates the proportion of new cases of malignancies in 2024, due to 12 infectious agents, reports progress in understanding the causes of cancer, as well as expanded and updated data on worldwide incidence. Different mechanisms explain why some infections increase the risk of cancer, adds BTA.. They can cause changes and mutations in the genes of infected cells, lead to chronic inflammation or seriously weaken the immune system. The cause of the majority of stomach cancers is infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which colonizes the stomach lining and leads to about 760,000 cases of cancer. In second place are human papillomaviruses (HPV, according to the English abbreviation), which are the cause of the most common sexually transmitted infections, as well as approximately 750,000 cases of cancer. Although the vast majority of papillomavirus infections are asymptomatic, about a dozen of these types can persist in the body and lead to cancer, for example of the cervix, anus, throat. The list also includes hepatitis B viruses, responsible for about 360,000 cases of cancer, and hepatitis C - for about 160,000. The main novelty in the study is the estimated impact of Epstein-Barr virus, responsible for about 260,000 case. "Epstein-Barr virus does not cause more cases of cancer, but advances in scientific knowledge allow for a better understanding of this scourge," says Dr. Clifford. This widespread member of the herpes family plays a role in the occurrence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, lymphomas, some types of stomach cancer, and more. Five pathogens - Helicobacter pylori (4 percent), human papillomavirus (4 percent), hepatitis B (2 percent), Epstein-Barr virus (1 percent), and hepatitis C (less than 1 percent) - cause almost all infectious cancers. However, significant global disparities still exist. East Asia accounts for 42 percent of new cases of infectious cancer, mainly caused by Helicobacter pylori and hepatitis B virus. Sub-Saharan Africa is also heavily affected, with 28.5 percent, particularly by papillomavirus and Kaposi's sarcoma virus. Overall, by 2024, more than three a quarter of infection-related cancers occur in low- and middle-income countries, where access to prevention and treatment remains uneven. Several "scientifically proven" strategies could prevent most of these cancers - vaccinations (against HPV and hepatitis B virus), screening and treatment (for Helicobacter pylori, viral hepatitis, HIV). Through vaccination, several rich countries appear to be on track to eliminate HPV infections within a few years, starting with Australia, which has set a goal of almost eliminating cervical cancer by 2035. However, in many regions of the world, preventive measures face persistent obstacles - financial, political or related to health systems, notes the International Agency for Research on Cancer. The WHO agency is also calling for the development of new tools, and in particular vaccines against the Epstein-Barr virus, for which there is currently no effective preventive measure. "Targeting new viruses, cancer-causing viruses may help prevent other diseases they cause, such as multiple sclerosis in the case of the Epstein-Barr virus, says Dr. Gary Clifford

and Acceptance of Human PapillomavirusVBaccination among Female Healthcare Students in Pakistan 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月02日 来源:Discover Public Health 1.3 编辑推荐: 背景:尽管宫颈癌负担较高,巴基斯坦人乳头瘤病毒(Human Papillomavirus, HPV)疫苗接种覆盖率仍极低。了解女性医疗卫生专业学生的态度与障碍,对于设计有效干预措施至关重要。目的:该质性研究探讨巴基斯坦女性医疗卫生专业学生对HPV疫苗接种的知识 欢迎领域“高通量小分子筛选解决方案”>> 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Research Open access 背景:尽管宫颈癌负担较高,巴基斯坦人乳头瘤病毒(Human Papillomavirus, HPV)疫苗接种覆盖率仍极低。了解女性医疗卫生专业学生的态度与障碍,对于设计有效干预措施至关重要。目的:该质性研究探讨巴基斯坦女性医疗卫生专业学生对HPV疫苗接种的知识、态度、犹豫驱动因素及建议策略。方法:该质性研究对巴基斯坦伊斯兰堡和拉瓦尔品第公立与私立机构的20名女性医学生进行面对面半结构化访谈。数据收集于2025年12月至2026年2月。依据Braun and Clarke框架进行归纳主题分析。结果:参与者普遍知道HPV疫苗可预防宫颈癌;然而,深入科学理解有限。多数人信任疫苗有效性,但许多人对政府主导的疫苗接种规划仍持怀疑态度,反映出新型冠状病毒肺炎(COVID-19)大流行后持续存在的机构不信任。医疗从业者,尤其是妇科医生,被视为疫苗接种建议最可靠来源。将HPV疫苗接种与不孕联系起来的误解被确定为主要文化障碍,甚至影响那些拒绝该说法的参与者。保护青少年女孩免于宫颈癌是疫苗接种接受度的最强动机之一。参与者偏好知情选择而非强制接种,并倡导文化适配的多渠道意识运动、宗教人士参与、大规模公众教育以及医疗从业者的可见支持,例如为其自身子女接种疫苗。结论:在该巴基斯坦女性医学生样本中,对HPV疫苗接种的认知常较表浅,并伴随机构不信任和持续的不孕相关误解。提高HPV疫苗接种接受度需要超出单纯认知的多方面策略,强调可信医疗从业者、开放沟通和文化敏感、基于研究的信息传递,以促进公众对免疫规划的信任。需要包含更多样化人群的额外质性和定量研究,以验证并扩展这些发现的普遍性。 研究背景与问题:人乳头瘤病毒(Human Papillomavirus, HPV)是全球最常见的性传播感染之一,但公众乃至医学生对HPV感染及其预防的认知仍不理想。宫颈癌是女性癌症相关发病和死亡的重要原因,2022年单年估计新增660 000例、死亡350 000例;低中收入国家(LMICs)负担更高,HPV疫苗、宫颈癌筛查和及时治疗可及性有限。世界卫生组织(WHO)推荐青少年女孩常规接种HPV疫苗作为宫颈癌一级预防基石,但南亚及WHO东南亚区域首剂HPV疫苗接种覆盖率偏低,部分国家尚未完全将HPV疫苗接种纳入国家免疫规划。巴基斯坦每年报告超过5 000例宫颈癌新发和超过3 000例死亡;既往研究提示认知有限、疫苗犹豫、经济限制以及缺乏政府资助的国家HPV疫苗接种规划是主要障碍,医学生中也存在类似知识缺口。巴基斯坦仍未消灭野生型脊髓灰质炎病毒,COVID-19疫苗接种过程也显示持续犹豫,假信息、宗教顾虑和副作用恐惧共同影响疫苗信心。巴基斯坦少于三分之二成人听说过HPV,仅3.1%曾接种HPV疫苗。因此,HPV疫苗接种不仅是医学问题,也是沟通和信任问题,需要社区为本、证据为基础的意识项目。该研究旨在探讨巴基斯坦女性医学/医疗卫生专业学生对HPV疫苗接种的认知、感知、接受度、犹豫驱动因素和推荐策略,并生成背景特异证据,以指导文化适配干预。 欢迎领取《抗体药研发解决方案》领 取 研究人员开展的研究、结论与意义:该研究采用解释主义质性研究,于2025年12月至2026年2月在伊斯兰堡和拉瓦尔品第的公立与私立高等教育机构招募20名女性医疗卫生专业学生,进行面对面半结构化访谈。参与者来自MBBS、Pharm-D、BDS、DPT和Psychology等学科,年龄20–25岁。通过归纳主题分析,研究人员发现:参与者对HPV疫苗预防宫颈癌有一般认知,但深层科学理解有限;多数信任疫苗有效性,却对政府主导疫苗规划存在机构不信任;医疗从业者,尤其妇科医生,是最可信建议来源;不孕相关误解是主要文化障碍;保护青少年女孩免于宫颈癌是接受疫苗的重要动机;参与者偏好知情选择而非强制接种,并建议文化适配、多渠道宣传、宗教人士参与、大规模公众教育和医疗从业者以身作则。研究结论强调,提高HPV疫苗接受度需多面策略,不仅增加认知,还要建立机构信任、开放沟通和文化敏感的信息传递。其意义在于为巴基斯坦HPV疫苗接种政策、医学教育和社区干预提供背景证据。 关键技术方法概括:该研究采用解释主义质性设计与便利抽样,样本来源为巴基斯坦伊斯兰堡和拉瓦尔品第公立及私立高等教育机构中20名20–25岁女性医疗卫生专业学生,学科涵盖MBBS、Pharm-D、BDS、DPT和Psychology;通过面对面半结构化访谈收集资料,访谈约15–20 min,持续至主题饱和。访谈指南经文献回顾、专家和心理师审查并预试验,由MA(MPhil)和ZI(Pharm D)实施,录音后逐字转录,经Urdu/English翻译与回译,采用Braun and Clarke六阶段归纳主题分析,研究者独立编码并讨论至共识;研究遵循COREQ,获Hamdard University伦理批准(Ref: ERC-FOP-09-06),参与者匿名编码R.01–R.20。 研究结果:3.1 HPV疫苗的基础知识(Foundational knowledge of the HPV vaccine)。3.1.1 疫苗认知的核心理解(Core understanding of vaccine awareness):访谈显示,多数参与者知道HPV疫苗可预防宫颈癌,但对其作用机制和长期安全性知识有限;少数能说明免疫机制,如暴露前刺激抗体产生,以及预防感染与降低癌症风险之间的直接联系。3.1.2 揭示知识缺口(Uncovering knowledge gaps):超过半数参与者承认自身HPV免疫知识不完整,仅少数自认知识充足;他们对长期效果、副作用和作用机制不确定,这种个人知识局限被反复视为犹豫来源,也提示教育干预机会。3.2 面对围绕HPV疫苗的信任与犹豫(Confronting trust and reluctance around the HPV vaccine)。3.2.1 对医疗专业人员的信任(Trust in healthcare professionals):参与者常提到医生建议可成为免疫决策的决定因素,妇科医生、家庭医生等可信医疗专业人员是接受疫苗的强大促进者,个人关系比大众媒体公告更有分量。3.2.2 免费疫苗困境(The free vaccine dilemma):参与者对免费HPV疫苗看法混合,许多人认为政府资助接种可提高可及性,尤其利于低收入家庭;但一些人将免费接种与机构不信任联系,受既往国家疫苗接种活动尤其是COVID-19影响,透明沟通资金、安全性和实施对建立信任至关重要。3.2.3 普遍的不孕恐惧(The prevailing fear of infertility):参与者一致认为HPV疫苗导致女性不孕是最常见、最有影响力的误解,跨人口学和教育组存在,并成为接受疫苗的主要障碍;即使拒绝该说法的参与者也承认其影响社区决策。3.2.4 纯洁性顾虑与隐藏议程(Purity concerns vs. Hidden agendas):误解还涉及HPV疫苗纯度与外国来源,如西方用疫苗进行人口控制的谣言,以及疫苗可能促进年轻女孩早期性行为的担忧;宗教神职人员有时被指为传播来源,提示需要尊重社区顾虑的文化敏感信息。3.3 促进对HPV疫苗接种的信任与意愿(Promoting trust and willingness for HPV vaccination)。3.3.1 预防作为核心动机(Prevention as a core motivation):保护年轻女性免于宫颈癌是最强动机,参与者将接种视为负责任、主动保护未来世代的选择,癌症严重性超过许多顾虑。3.3.2 知情选择优先于强制政策(Prioritizing informed choice over mandatory policy):多数参与者认为无认知的强迫会造成不信任和反对,应通过良好信息说服公众而非强制,这反映父母权威等文化价值;少数认为初期应个人选择,意识运动后应强制。3.3.3 导致疫苗拒绝的决定因素(Determinants leading to vaccine refusal):确认严重副作用是最强拒绝原因;可信医生建议不接种也会导致拒绝;指南不清、缺乏证据和信息模糊足以产生怀疑并拒绝,说明拒绝常基于具体、可解决的顾虑而非完全反对。3.4 提高HPV疫苗接种接受度的推荐方法(Recommended approaches to enhance HPV vaccination acceptance)。3.4.1 实施多层次教育策略(Implementing multi-level educational strategies):参与者建议使用多沟通渠道,电视面向依赖传统媒体的老年人,社交媒体包括Instagram、Facebook、TikTok和WhatsApp面向青年,学校、学院意识会议和清真寺布道也被提及,并分享他国成功故事以建立信心。3.4.2 动员可信声音促进认知(Mobilizing trusted voices to promote awareness):除医疗从业者外,参与者强烈建议纳入宗教和社区领袖,因其影响力大;先教育这些领袖,使其公开支持,可弥合官方信息与社区接受之间的差距。3.4.3 用科学证据替代误解(Replacing misconceptions with scientific evidence):参与者报告,不孕恐惧等公众误解必须在所有意识活动中直接、科学地处理,科学解释应说明HPV疫苗为何不影响生育,医生应准备在咨询中回答此类问题。3.4.4 通过行动和证据建立信心(Building confidence through action and evidence):参与者建议医疗人员和官员先给自己的孩子接种,以展示对HPV疫苗安全性的真实信心;卫生部长给女儿接种等可见行动可鼓励公众,个人榜样比单纯统计更有效。 讨论部分总结:该研究提供质性证据,表明女性医学生对HPV疫苗的接受度受知识、机构信任、错误信息和对医疗提供者信心共同影响。虽然参与者普遍承认疫苗预防宫颈癌的作用,但对其更广泛益处和安全性仍有知识缺口。研究结果显示,提高HPV疫苗接受度需超越增加认知,强调信任建设、文化敏感沟通和可信医疗从业者参与,这与既往质性研究一致。参与者区分对疫苗科学有效性的信心与对实施机构信任,说明接受度依赖对卫生系统的信任。医疗提供者,尤其医生,被视为最可信信息来源。不孕相关误解是最有影响力障碍之一,许多参与者个人否认但承认其在社区中的影响。宫颈癌预防是主要益处,参与者偏好知情决策而非强制接种。安全顾虑和证据不足进一步提示透明沟通及医疗提供者明确建议的重要性。成功项目需医疗从业者、社区领袖和宗教影响者协调沟通。意义方面,卫生课程应加强HPV感染和疫苗接种教育,接种项目应优先医疗提供者主导沟通,并主动用清晰、文化适配、基于研究的信息解决误解,尤其不孕顾虑;该研究优势是聚焦未来疫苗接种倡导和社区健康促进中重要的女性医学生群体。 研究结论(Conclusion)翻译:这项针对巴基斯坦女性医学学生的质性研究强调,HPV疫苗接种知识主要局限于其预防宫颈癌的作用,对其更大的科学和公共卫生益处理解有限。尽管参与者表现出对疫苗有效性的信心,许多人仍对政府主导的疫苗接种规划持怀疑态度,反映出COVID-19大流行后挥之不去的机构不信任。医疗从业者被视为最可靠的疫苗信息来源,而将HPV疫苗接种与不孕联系起来的误解被发现是主要社会文化限制。尽管有这些保留,保护青少年女孩免于宫颈癌仍是疫苗接种接受的强烈动机。参与者主张知情决策而非强制接种,并强调需要由可信医疗从业者、社区领袖和宗教领袖传递透明、文化适配、多渠道沟通。总之,这些发现表明,提高HPV疫苗接种接受度需要增强知识、建立机构信任并处理社会文化顾虑的策略,以促进巴基斯坦HPV疫苗接种规划的成功实施。 supplementary_news.content: Saturday, October 3 2026 Home Contacts Press Office Advertising Info Banner Advertising Electoral Advertising Editorial Staff Music Social Media Managers Association Contributions 2021 Contributions 2022 Contributions 2023 Contributions 2024 Contributions 2025 Archive Menu Search for Home Exhibitions Meetings Music Books Cinema Theater University Interviews Podcast English Italiano English Español Deutsch Русский Français العربية 中文 (中国) Português Passaggi d'Autore - Intrecci mediterranei | Sant'Antioco 3-8 dicembre 2025 Home/Health/HPV prevention: six open days in Oristano Health HPV prevention: six open days in Oristano Sonia Sarra2 days ago 13 4 minutes read Pap tests and vaccination against papillomavirus will be available at the San Martino hospital in six days dedicated to prevention and female health. HPV prevention At the center of six Open Days organized by the ASL 5 of Oristano. The initiative will start on Friday 9 October and will allow access to the Pap test without reservation. On the same days it will also be possible to receive vaccination against papillomavirus, according to the criteria indicated by the ASL campaign. The appointments will be held in the gynecology clinics of the San Martino hospital, on the fourth floor of the P Corps. The goal is to make it easier to access two important prevention tools. Free Pap Test in Oristano The pap smear will be offered free of charge to women up to 64 as part of the initiative. Reservations will not be required for Open Days: it will be sufficient to go directly to the hospital. The days dedicated to the exam are Friday 9, 16 and 23 October, from 2 pm to 7 pm, and Saturday 10, 17 and 24 October, from 8.30 to 13. A day is also provided for employees of the ASL 5. additional Friday 2 October, from 9 to 13. To access the service, it is necessary to bring the health card and, if received, the invitation letter from the Screening Center. HPV prevention and early diagnosis Cervical cervical cancer is closely linked to persistent infection from some types of human papillomavirus. The Ministry of Health indicates anti-HPV vaccination and screening among the fundamental tools to reduce risk and detect any alterations early. The Pap test allows you to analyze cells taken from the uterine cervix. Based on age and the regional program, screening can include the Pap test or the HPV-DNA test. At the national level, the ministry indicates the Pap test every three years between 25 and 29 years and the HPV test every five years from 30 to 64 years, with differences related to the regional organization of programs. Who can participate in the Open Days The ASL 5 initiative expands access to the normal screening path. In fact, the press release from the health company indicates that, during the Open Days, the Pap test will also be offered to young people under 25 who have already had sexual relations for at least a year. For minors, the preference for the presence of a companion is indicated. For women included in the ordinary range of screening, it remains important to follow the instructions received from their ASL. The organized programs are in fact free prevention courses aimed at the population in the foreseen age groups. Papillomavirus vaccination Alongside the test, anti-HPV vaccination will be available. According to what was communicated by the ASL of Oristano, during the six days the vaccination will be offered free of charge in the range indicated by the company, from 11 to 30 years. Vaccination is one of the tools for preventing HPV infection. The Ministry of Health indicates the twelfth year of life as the recommended age for vaccination, both for girls and boys. However, vaccination does not replace screening. In fact, the ministry points out that vaccinated women must also follow the planned control programs, because the vaccine does not protect against all types of high-risk HPV. How to prepare for the Pap Test To prevent some factors from interfering with the examination, the ASL of Oristano indicates some precautions. The test should be done away from menstruation, at least five days before or five days after their conclusion. In the previous three days it is also indicated to avoid sexual intercourse. In the 48 hours before the examination, however, it is necessary to avoid vaginal washes, eggs, creams, gels, foams and spermicides. These are the information provided by the health company for open days. In case of personal doubts or particular conditions, it is advisable to contact health professionals. HPV prevention, a path that continues The Open Days are part of the ordinary activities of the Prevention Department of the ASL 5. The health authority offers vaccination against HPV through the hygiene and public health clinics. The October campaign therefore aims to put vaccination and screening together in the same path. The idea is to reduce obstacles to access and offer a concrete opportunity to get information and adhere to prevention activities. The Ministry of Health considers oncological screening public health interventions aimed at identifying early tumors or lesions that can precede them, through organized and free paths. dates, times and information The appointments will take place at the San Martino hospital in Oristano, in the gynecology clinics of the fourth floor, Corpo P. The calendar includes Friday 9, 16 and 23 October from 2 pm to 7 pm and Saturday 10, 17 and 24 October from 8.30 to 13. An additional day is scheduled for employees of the ASL 5 on Friday 2 October from 9 to 13. For information, it is possible to contact the gynecology and obstetrics unit at 0783 317205 and 0783 317227. For general vaccination modalities, the ASL 5 also indicates its clinics of hygiene and public health. The initiative thus offers an additional opportunity to get information and access health services. The HPV prevention, together with participation in screening programs and vaccination when indicated, represents an important part of cervical cancer prevention. Pap tests and vaccination against papillomavirus will be available at the San Martino hospital in six days dedicated to prevention and female health. Croatia at around 50 percent vaccination rate for children against HPV Portal.hr 01. Oct 2026. 12:57 Share on FacebookShare via WhatsAppShare online X Croatia is at around 50 percent vaccination rate for children against HPV, while the World Health Organization's goal is coverage of more than 90 percent, which is one of the key prerequisites for eliminating cervical cancer, it was said on Thursday at a symposium dedicated to the disease. Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection affects both sexes and can cause premalignant and malignant changes in the anogenital area and head and neck tumors. In Croatia, about 50 percent of children under the age of 15 are now vaccinated, epidemiologist Željka Karin pointed out at the symposium "Cervical Cancer - Prevent the Cause, Eliminate the Consequences", which brought together experts from several medical fields at the Clinic for Infectious Diseases "Dr. Fran Mihaljević". TEXT CONTINUES BELOW ADVERTISEMENT "The vaccine is safe and protects against HPV-related cancers in about 90 percent of cases," said Karin. According to the Croatian Institute of Public Health, around 300 women in Croatia develop cervical cancer each year, and around 120 die. Almost all cases of the disease are linked to infection with high-risk types of HPV. According to the World Health Organization, this accounts for around 99 percent of cases. HPV vaccination in Croatia is free for children and young people from the fifth grade of primary school to the age of 25. Children are actively encouraged to get vaccinated before the age of 15, when there is a better immune response. School children and students can be vaccinated by a school physician, and others by an epidemiologist. Vaccination is also possible after the age of 25 if there is a medical indication and a recommendation from a specialist. TEXT CONTINUES BELOW ADVERTISEMENT Sweden with vaccination rate up to 90 percent Scientist Laila Sara Arroyo Mühr from the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm presented the experience of Sweden, where children are vaccinated against HPV in schools at the age of 11. Coverage for girls is around 90 percent and for boys around 85 percent. Swedish experience shows that vaccination uptake is higher when vaccination is organised through a school programme than when children and parents have to make their own appointments. In the programme for older girls, who had to make their own appointments, vaccination uptake was around 60 per cent, significantly lower than in the school programme. Arroyo Mühr emphasized that simple access, direct appeals, and trust in health recommendations are important for higher vaccination rates. She said that among young people, who delivers the message is often more important than the message itself, so doctors, nurses, pharmacists, parents, peers, and teachers play an important role in promoting vaccination. TEXT CONTINUES BELOW ADVERTISEMENT She also emphasized that it is best to get vaccinated before starting sexual activity because the vaccine prevents new infections, but does not treat an existing infection. Without screening, there is no rapid elimination of the disease. Professor Mario Poljak from Ljubljana warned that around 12 percent of all malignant tumors in the world are related to infections, and around four percent of all tumors to HPV, which means approximately 750.000 new cases annually. He pointed out that high vaccination rates alone will not lead to the elimination of cervical cancer quickly enough. According to the models he presented, 90 percent vaccination of girls and boys by age 15 could lead to the elimination of cervical cancer in about a hundred years. If such vaccination is combined with screening, the goal could be reached about 60 years earlier. Poljak therefore emphasized that vaccination and screening must go hand in hand and that screening will remain necessary for decades to come. Modern screening should be based on HPV testing, but not all HPV tests available on the market are suitable for this purpose, only clinically validated ones. TEXT CONTINUES BELOW ADVERTISEMENT The symposium was organized by the Croatian Academy of Medical Sciences, whose president Alemka Markotić pointed out that cervical cancer continues to claim women's lives, although much can be done through prevention. In a video address, Health Minister Irena Hrstić highlighted the improvement of preventive programs and early detection of diseases among the main challenges. Le Fact checked by: Spencer Feldman Listen 0:00 / 0:00 Key Takeaways Six-month VHNSSv2 outcomes favored 54 Gy, including less worsening in solid-food swallowing (median +1.38 vs +3.31) and no increase in voice problems (0.0 vs +1.0). Additional symptom domains improved with 54 Gy, including swallowing liquids, xerostomia, and neck/shoulder mobility, with effect sizes suggesting nonrandom variation despite limited standard-dose sample size. E1308 enrolled stage III–IVB, predominantly nonsmoking patients; 78% achieved complete clinical response after paclitaxel/cisplatin/cetuximab induction and received 54 Gy IMRT plus weekly cetuximab. Safety signals favored deintensification, with lower rates of grade ≥3 mucositis (30% vs 47%) and dysphagia (15% vs 29%), while grade 4 events remained <5% in both arms. Interpretation is limited by nonrandom dose assignment, only nine standard-dose patients, attrition in later PRO time points, and cross-trial comparisons confounded by HPV heterogeneity and differing radiation techniques. SHOW MORE Patients with HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer who received 23% less radiation reported fewer swallowing, voice and dry mouth problems six months after treatment. Advertisement Patients with human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal cancer, a cancer in the middle part of the throat, may have fewer swallowing and voice problems with a lower dose of radiation. Six months after treatment, patients who responded well to chemotherapy and received less radiation reported fewer symptoms than those who received the standard dose. The results come from an analysis of two phase 2 trials run by the ECOG-ACRIN Cancer Research Group, published in JCO Oncology Advances. The earlier trial, E2399, found that patients with HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer had higher response rates and longer survival than patients whose cancer was not linked to HPV. Those results fueled interest in treatment that keeps cure rates high with fewer short- and long-term side effects. The follow-up trial, E1308, tested whether patients whose tumors disappeared on exam after chemotherapy could receive 54 gray (Gy), the unit used to measure radiation dose, instead of the standard 69.3 Gy. The researchers noted that the 23% reduction could ease long-term swallowing problems, taste changes, mucus production and dry mouth. What did the E1308 trial find about swallowing and voice after lower-dose radiation? Six months after treatment, patients who received 54 Gy reported less difficulty swallowing solid food on the Vanderbilt Head and Neck Symptom Survey Version 2 (VHNSSv2), a 50-item questionnaire in which patients rate head and neck cancer symptoms from 0 (none) to 10 (severe). Scores for swallowing solids rose by a median of 1.38 points from before treatment in the lower-dose group, compared with 3.31 points in the standard-dose group. Voice problems did not increase with the lower dose (0.0) but rose by 1.0 point with the standard dose. The lower-dose group also reported less trouble swallowing liquids, less dry mouth and fewer limits in moving the neck and shoulders. Scores for the lower-dose and standard-dose groups were 0.0 and 0.5, respectively, for swallowing liquids; 3.5 and 5.1 for dry mouth; and 0.0 and 1 for neck and shoulder movement. These differences were large enough that chance was an unlikely explanation. A second questionnaire, the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Head & Neck (FACT-HN), showed a smaller drop in voice strength and quality with the lower dose. The same survey showed less difficulty eating solid food in the lower-dose group, although that gap fell short of the level researchers use to rule out chance. Scores for mouth pain, nutrition, excess mucus, taste and smell changes and teeth problems were also lower with 54 Gy. The researchers described those differences as clinically important, but the gaps could have come about by chance, likely because few patients received the standard dose. “The cardinal finding of this analysis is that swallowing dysfunction and oral symptoms are very prevalent early after [chemotherapy and radiation] but less evident at later time points,” wrote the researchers. At 12 months, 40% of patients who received the lower dose rated their difficulty swallowing solids at 2 or higher on the survey's 0-to-10 scale, compared with 89% of patients who received the standard dose. Nutrition problems at that level affected 10% and 44% of patients, respectively. Fewer patients completed the surveys at later time points, so the researchers focused their results on the six-month mark. Broader quality-of-life surveys, which measured fatigue, physical activity and the ability to handle daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, shopping and cooking, did not detect differences between the dose groups at any time point. According to the researchers, the surveys designed for head and neck cancer were better at capturing changes in side effects. How did lower-dose radiation on E1308 compare with the radiation used on E2399? E2399 treated 69 patients with oropharyngeal cancer, including cancers linked and not linked to HPV. Patients received paclitaxel and carboplatin before radiation, followed by 70 Gy of three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy (3DRT) over seven weeks with weekly paclitaxel. E1308 used intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), a highly targeted form of radiation, and patients in the lower-dose group received 54 Gy over 5.5 weeks. In an exploratory comparison of patients whose cancer had not progressed 12 months after treatment, patients on E1308 reported no decline from before treatment in their ability to eat solid food or to eat the foods they liked on the FACT-HN. Patients on E2399 reported a decline on both measures. Who was in the E1308 trial of lower-dose radiation for HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer? E1308 included 80 eligible patients with stage 3 to 4b HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer that could be removed with surgery. The median age was 57, and 84% were not current smokers. Patients first received three cycles of induction chemotherapy, or chemotherapy given before radiation, with paclitaxel and cisplatin plus Erbitux (cetuximab). The trial assigned 54 Gy of IMRT with weekly Erbitux to patients whose main tumor disappeared on physical exam after chemotherapy, called a complete clinical response, and the standard 69.3 Gy of IMRT with weekly Erbitux to patients without a complete response. A total of 62 patients (78%) received the lower dose. Among patients who received the lower dose, the two-year progression-free survival rate, meaning the share of patients alive without their cancer growing or spreading, was 81%. Among patients who did not have a complete response and received 69.3 Gy, the two-year progression-free survival rate was 65%. Patients completed symptom surveys before treatment and at six, 12, 24 and 30 months after treatment. The survey analysis included 51 patients whose cancer had not progressed at 12 months, nine of whom received the standard dose and 42 the lower dose. What side effects did patients have with lower-dose radiation on the E1308 trial? Patients who received 69.3 Gy with Erbitux had more frequent grade 3 or higher mouth sores, known as mucositis, than patients who received 54 Gy (47% versus 30%). The standard-dose group also had more difficulty swallowing (29% versus 15%), acne-like rash (24% versus 12%), skin irritation from radiation (12% versus 7%), blood clots (6% versus 0%) and low levels of lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell (35% versus 12%). Grade 4 side effects occurred in fewer than 5% of patients in each dose group. Compared with patients who received 54 Gy on E1308, patients who received 3DRT on E2399 had more grade 3 or higher mouth sores (58% versus 29%), difficulty swallowing (39% versus 15%), inflammation of the esophagus (8% versus 0%) and infections (8% versus 0%). Patients who received the lower dose on E1308 had more grade 3 or higher low lymphocyte counts (13% versus 3%), which the researchers attributed to the more intensive three-drug chemotherapy given before radiation. What are the limitations of the E1308 radiation dose study? Only nine patients received the standard dose, which limited some comparisons between groups. Fewer patients completed the surveys at later time points, possibly because of the time the questionnaires took, and some patients left the analysis by 12 months because their cancer came back or because of other events. Patients were not assigned to their dose groups at random. The comparison with E2399 also included patients whose cancer was not linked to HPV, which the researchers noted introduces variation and potential bias. The two radiation techniques also differ in tumor margins, dose to the salivary glands and throat muscles used for swallowing, and risk of lymphedema, or swelling. “Ultimately, adequately powered randomized trials using appropriate [patient-reported outcome] instruments will be needed to determine the optimal approaches for HPV-related disease,” the researchers concluded. References Cmelak AJ, et al. “Patient-Reported Toxicity With Radiation Deintensification in Human Papillomavirus–Associated Oropharynx Cancer: ECOG-ACRIN E2399 and E1308.” JCO Oncology Advances.
